title: How to Cleanse and Charge Crystals
description: Learn nine ways to cleanse and charge crystals, from smoke and sound to moonlight and selenite, plus which stones must never touch water, salt or sun.
html:
Every crystal collector eventually asks the same question: how often should I cleanse my stones, and what is the right way to do it? The tradition is simple. Crystals are believed to take on the energy of the places and people around them, so practitioners clear them from time to time, much as you might open the windows in a stuffy room. There is no single correct ritual, but there are a few hard physical limits, because a method that suits a tough quartz point can ruin a soft or water-sensitive stone.

This guide walks through nine common methods, explains the difference between cleansing and charging, and tells you which stones to keep away from each technique.

Cleansing versus charging

Cleansing is about clearing. Many people describe it as wiping the slate clean after a stone has been handled a lot, bought secondhand, or kept in a tense room. Charging is about refreshing a stone with energy, usually from the moon, the sun, the earth, or a larger crystal. Most practitioners cleanse first and charge second, then set an intention if they wish (see our guide on programming a crystal with an intention).

Several methods do both jobs at once. Moonlight and selenite are the best known examples.

How often should you cleanse?

Traditions vary, but a loose rhythm works for most people:

  • When you first bring a stone home, especially from a shop or a market where many hands have held it.
  • After a period of heavy use, such as a long meditation season or wearing a pendant daily.
  • When a stone simply feels dull or heavy to you. This is entirely personal.
  • Around a new moon or full moon, if you like to work with lunar cycles.

Do not feel you must clear everything weekly. Pieces on a display shelf may only need attention a few times a year.

Cleansing methods at a glance

Water

Rinsing under a cool stream is the oldest method and the one most likely to cause damage. It suits hard, non-porous stones such as Clear Quartz, Smoky Quartz and Jasper. A quick rinse, a gentle dry, and you are done.

Keep water away from Selenite, which is gypsum and dissolves, and from Halite, which is salt. Calcite, Fluorite, Malachite, Turquoise, Lapis Lazuli, Opal and Pearl can be dulled, stained or weakened. Our water safety guide explains why in detail.

Salt

Dry sea salt, or a salt bath, is popular and also hard on most stones. Salt is abrasive and corrosive, and it creeps into tiny cracks and pores. If you want to use it, limit it to rugged quartz and leave the stone in for minutes, not days. A safer habit is to place a stone on a dish beside a bowl of salt, never touching it.

Never use salt with metal-bearing stones such as Hematite and Pyrite, which can rust or tarnish, or with anything set in jewelry.

Smoke

Smoke cleansing, often with dried sage, palo santo, cedar or sweetgrass, is the most forgiving option. Hold the stone in the smoke for a few breaths while you think of clearing. Because nothing touches the surface, it is safe for every mineral. Smudge in a ventilated room, keep a fireproof dish nearby, and consider that some traditions ask for respectful sourcing of sacred plants. Incense or a few pinches of dried lavender work as alternatives if smoke bothers you or someone in your household.

Sound

A singing bowl, tuning fork, bell or even a few claps can be used to clear a stone. Sound cleansing is suited to fragile pieces because it requires no contact. Place the stone near the source and let the vibration ring through. Some people hum or chant instead, which has the advantage of costing nothing.

Moonlight

Setting stones on a windowsill overnight, especially under a full moon, is the gentlest way to clear and charge together. Moonlight is considered soothing and receptive, which suits calming stones like Moonstone, Amethyst and Rose Quartz. It will not fade colors. If rain or frost is forecast, bring delicate pieces inside, and keep them off rooftops and garden walls where they might fall.

Sunlight

Sunlight is considered a strong, energizing charge, popular with Carnelian, Tiger's Eye and Clear Quartz. It is also the quickest way to ruin a stone. Amethyst, Rose Quartz, Kunzite, Citrine (especially heat-treated pieces), Fluorite and Celestite can fade with long exposure. Many also crack from sudden heat if left behind glass. If you use sunlight, give it 15 to 30 minutes in early morning light and no more.

Selenite and cluster cleansing

Many collectors rest their stones on a selenite plate, wand or a Clear Quartz or Apophyllite cluster. It is dry, low effort and does not harm the stones. Leave pieces on the plate overnight. Selenite is soft and can scratch with a fingernail, so avoid grinding hard stones against it and do not let it sit in damp places.

Earth burial

Burying stones in a garden or large pot of clean soil for a day or a full moon cycle is a long-standing practice for connecting with the earth. It works best with dense, tumbled stones. The risks are practical: you can forget where you buried them, soil moisture can mark porous stones, and fertilizers or pesticides can stain. Use a bag or cloth for protection and mark the spot. Skip it for soft or sulfide stones, and for anything delicate or valuable.

Breath

The simplest ritual of all. Hold the stone in cupped hands, take a slow breath in, and exhale across it with the intention of clearing. It costs nothing, requires no equipment, and suits pieces that no other method can touch. Many practitioners use it for jewelry and travel stones.

Stones that need extra care

As a quick reference:

  • Soft or soluble: Selenite, Halite, Desert Rose and Angelite. Use smoke, sound or moonlight only.
  • Fade in light: Amethyst, Rose Quartz, Kunzite, Fluorite. Choose moonlight or sound.
  • Porous or treated: Turquoise, Opal, Howlite, Amber. Stay with smoke, sound and breath.
  • Copper-bearing and toxic: Malachite, Azurite, Chrysocolla. Never in water, and wash your hands after handling.
  • Metallic: Hematite, Pyrite, Magnetite. Keep dry and away from salt.

Building a simple routine

A practical routine for most collections looks like this. Wipe dusty stones with a dry cloth. Pass them through smoke or ring a bell over them. Leave the whole group on a windowsill under the next full moon, and store them afterwards in a cloth or box. That one evening covers every stone in a mixed collection without risking any of them.

Above all, trust your own sense of when a stone is ready. The methods matter less than the care and attention you bring.

Crystals are used for personal ritual and wellbeing practice, and they complement but never replace professional medical care.
